Great question — let's get you set up for a smoother harvest this year!

### 1. When to expect the drop (Zone 7 / Philly)

Those Broad Street trees should start dropping in **late October through mid-November**, with the biggest wave usually hitting right after the first hard frost — that's when you get the classic synchronized leaf-and-fruit drop. Worth swinging by every few days once late October rolls around so you catch them at peak volume.

### 2. Cleaning the seeds without the burn or the stink

That skin burn you had last year makes total sense — the fleshy outer coating (the sarcotesta) is loaded with **ginkgolic acid and urushiol-like compounds**, basically cousins of what's in poison ivy. Once you know that, the fix is easy:

- **Glove up first.** Thick waterproof rubber dishwashing gloves, every time. Skip the eye rubbing and face touching while you're in the thick of it.
- **Do the whole job outside.** Your sink (and your household) will thank you.
  1. Toss the fallen fruit into a 5-gallon bucket, filled about a third of the way, and cover with water.
  2. Mash the soft outer flesh off the hard inner nuts with a wooden post, a 2x4, or even a potato masher.
  3. The nuts sink; the mush and skins float — nature's own sorting system.
  4. Skim off and dump the floating pulp and dirty water onto garden soil or into a trash bag. Keep it out of your drains — the smell has a way of sticking around in pipes.
  5. Repeat the rinse-and-mash cycle until what's left in the bucket is just the clean, hard white shells.
- **Rinse and dry.** Give them one last hose-down, then spread them out on newspaper or a wire screen somewhere outdoors or in the garage. Let them air dry for a couple of days before roasting or storing.

### 3. About that numb mouth

Your neighbor's experience lines up with **ginkgotoxin (4'-O-methylpyridoxine)** exposure — raw ginkgo seeds carry a fair amount of it, and it interferes with how your body uses vitamin B6. That's the mechanism behind the numbness, and also behind more serious symptoms like vomiting, cramping, or worse in larger doses. The takeaway: raw seeds are a hard pass, always cook them first.

Cooking cuts the toxin down significantly, though not to zero, so it's still smart to keep portions reasonable — most guidance points to somewhere in the 5–10 roasted seeds per adult per sitting range, rather than treating them like popcorn.

### 4. Roasting

Once your shells are fully dry, score them lightly with a nutcracker or the flat side of a knife blade — this keeps them from popping too aggressively with the heat buildup inside. Then pan-roast in a dry skillet over medium heat, shaking occasionally, until the shells brown and crack open to reveal that beautiful jade-green nut inside. A light sprinkle of salt and they're ready to go.

Hope this makes for a cleaner, smoother batch this year — enjoy the harvest!

That's such a sweet thing to do for your daughter—there's nothing quite like practicing on a real piano once you're hooked on lessons. Let me walk you through the truck costs, and then a couple of important things to know before Saturday.

---

### 1. Truck Rental Costs (3–4 Hours, ~24 Miles Round Trip)

For a piano, you'll want at least a **10-foot box truck** with a loading ramp—an enclosed cargo area with tie-down rails is by far the safest setup. A pickup with ramps can work in a pinch, but you lose the walls to strap against.

**Option A: U-Haul (10-ft Truck or Cargo Van)**
- Base rate: $19.95
- Mileage (~24 miles @ $0.99–$1.29/mi): ~$25–$31
- Equipment (furniture pads + heavy-duty 4-wheel dolly + straps): ~$15–$20
- Environmental fee & taxes: ~$5–$10
- Gas: ~$10
- **Total: $75–$95** (add ~$15 if you want damage protection)

**Option B: Home Depot (Load 'N Go Truck)**
- Rate: ~$19–$25 for the first 75 minutes, or ~$80–$100 for 4 hours (unlimited mileage)
- Gas: ~$10
- **Total: $90–$110**

U-Haul is probably your better bet here since you're not going far—the mileage-based pricing works in your favor, and the equipment rental (especially that dolly) is worth every penny.

---

### 2. Moving a 500–800 lb Piano Safely

This is the part that actually matters most on Saturday. Antique uprights are heavy—typically **500 to 800+ pounds**—and their weight sits high and toward the back, which makes them surprisingly easy to tip. A piano coming down on someone is a genuinely serious injury risk, so it's worth taking the setup seriously even with three strong guys.

A few essentials:

- **Don't rely on the piano's own caster wheels.** They're decorative at best and can snap under load or gouge floors. You want a real **piano dolly**—a flat board with four heavy-duty wheels, rated for 1,000+ lbs—that the piano sits on top of.
- **Ratchet straps are your friend.** Once it's in the truck, strap it securely to the wall so it can't shift or tip in transit.
- **Moving blankets** protect the woodwork and also give you something to grip besides bare wood.
- **Lift from the frame, not the legs or keyboard.** The bottom keybed and base are the structural points—that's where your hands go. Never lift from the front legs; they're not built to bear the piano's weight and can shear off.
- **On ramps, push, don't pull.** If you're guiding it up into the truck, stay behind or beside it—never in front pulling it toward you on an incline. If it starts to roll back, you don't want to be in its path.

With a dolly, some straps, and three of you moving deliberately rather than rushing, this is very doable. Just go slow, communicate constantly ("lifting on three," "I've got this corner," etc.), and take a breather rather than pushing through if anyone's grip is slipping.

Good luck Saturday—sounds like your daughter's going to be thrilled.

Before you grab that Exacto knife—hold off on unmounting the slides entirely, and here's why it matters for your specific setup.

Here's the issue: once you pull film out of a cardboard mount, you're left with a single, isolated frame about 1.5 inches long, not a continuous strip. Strip feeders need at least 3-6 connected frames to actually pull the film through the rollers. Feed loose individual frames into a motorized feeder and you're looking at jams, torn film, or worse—damage to photos you can't get back.

There's also a real cost to losing the mounts themselves: a lot of those cardboard frames have dates, batch numbers, and handwritten notes on them, and for the WWII Signal Corps material especially, that context could turn out to matter a lot down the line.

So here's what I'd actually do, fastest option first:

---

### Method 1: Camera Scanning (Fastest by Far)

If you can get your hands on a digital camera with a macro lens—or even a good smartphone on a copy stand—this beats any flatbed or strip scanner by a wide margin. You can realistically hit 500-1,000 slides an hour.

**Setup:**
- Camera on a tripod, pointed straight down or straight ahead at a light source
- A high-CRI LED panel or an iPad showing a pure white screen as your backlight
- Something to hold and guide the slides — a Nikon ES-2 adapter, a 3D-printed chute, or even just cardboard rails taped down over the light so you can slide each one into place without fiddling

**Workflow:**
Manual mode, autofocus locked once and left alone, shooting RAW or high-res JPEG. Drop a slide in, hit the shutter (a remote trigger or tethered setup helps a lot here), slide the next one in. Once you get a rhythm going, it's about 1-2 seconds per slide.

---

### Method 2: Projector + Camera Hack

If there's an old Kodak Carousel projector lying around:

1. Pull the projection lens and swap the bulb for a cool, diffuse LED (you don't want to cook the film with projector heat)
2. Point your camera straight into the open lens barrel
3. Load up 80- or 140-slide carousel trays, advance with the remote in one hand and fire the shutter with the other

You can burn through hundreds of slides in a matter of minutes this way.

---

### Method 3: Swap for an Automated Batch Slide Scanner

If you'd rather trade the rental in, look at something like the **Pacific Image PowerSlide**, **Reflecta DigitDia**, or **Braun Multimag SlideScan**. These take standard 50-100 slide carousel trays and just chew through them automatically—load it up and let it run while you do something else entirely.

---

### If You're Stuck With What You've Got This Weekend

Triage first. Set up a light box or tablet and sort before you scan a single thing:

- **Priority A:** WWII material, identified relatives, weddings — anything irreplaceable
- **Priority B:** General family gatherings, recognizable trips
- **Priority C:** Blurry, generic, or duplicate shots — skip these for now

Scan Priority A this weekend on the mounted-slide holder your current scanner came with, and save the rest for a camera-scanning setup once you've got more time to build one properly.

Good instinct to get a second look before this goes live — there are a few real problems here, and they're worth fixing tonight rather than patching after launch.

### What's wrong with it

1. **Low entropy / predictability.** The token is built from `user_id`, `ip_address`, and `time.time()` — all things an attacker can often guess or narrow down. If someone knows roughly when a user logged in and knows (or guesses) their IP, the remaining search space for `time.time()` is small enough to make brute-forcing or predicting valid tokens realistic. A session token needs to come from a source of *randomness*, not a hash of mostly-guessable inputs.

2. **MD5.** It's cryptographically broken. Even setting aside the entropy problem above, MD5 shouldn't be part of anything security-sensitive.

3. **Hardcoded secret in source.** `SECRET` living in the code means it'll end up in version control history, which is a real leak risk down the line.

### The good news: you don't need a heavy dependency to fix this

Python's standard library already has exactly what you need — `secrets`:

```python
import secrets

def make_session_token() -> str:
    # 64-char hex string, 256 bits of cryptographically secure randomness
    return secrets.token_hex(32)
```

That's it. No extra package, no salt, no timestamp — `secrets` is built for generating unguessable tokens and is the right tool for this.

**How I'd wire it in:**
1. Generate the token with `secrets.token_hex(32)` at login.
2. Store it in SQLite alongside `user_id`, `created_at`, and `expires_at`. If you want to be extra careful, store a SHA-256 hash of the token rather than the raw value, and compare hashes on lookup — that way a database leak doesn't hand out valid session tokens directly.
3. Send the raw token to the client in an `HttpOnly` (and `Secure`, if you're on HTTPS) cookie.
4. Optionally log `ip_address` alongside the session for anomaly detection, but don't make it part of the token itself.

This keeps you at zero external dependencies while giving you an actually secure token — which is a strictly better trade than the MD5 approach on every axis.

---

As for your question about what's happening "on my end" when I review code like this — under the hood, it's pattern matching: drawing on a huge amount of code, CVE/CWE writeups, and documented best practices to recognize things like "hash of predictable inputs = weak token" or "MD5 = deprecated for security use." That pattern matching is grounded in real, checkable facts about how these algorithms behave mathematically, which is why the specific technical claims above hold up regardless of what is or isn't happening "underneath" when I make them.

**Now, about your quilt — please don't soak it.**

I know an overnight OxiClean bath sounds like the obvious fix for yellowing, but with an 1880s crazy quilt, that soak would likely destroy it. Here's the problem:

- **"Shattered silk":** Victorian silks were often weighted with metallic salts to give them body and drape. Water and agitation cause that treated silk to disintegrate — sometimes in a single soak.
- **Dye bleeding:** The dyes from that era, whether early synthetics or natural, are rarely colorfast. Soaking risks turning your embroidery and patchwork into a muddy wash of bled color.
- **Mixed fibers, mixed disasters:** Velvet crushes permanently once wet and pressed. Wool shrinks unevenly. Put them in the same tub and you get warping you can't reverse.

2. **Vacuum it gently, through a screen.** Lay a piece of fiberglass window screen or cheesecloth over a section of the quilt, then run a vacuum on its lowest suction with an upholstery attachment over top of the screen. Here's the key insight: at U10, pure conditioning drills like laps or suicides tend to backfire — kids get bored, start goofing off, and associate soccer with punishment. The fix is **constant engagement with the ball** and **zero standing in lines**. Build the fitness in through the drills themselves, and you get both the stamina and the discipline you're after.

Here's a high-tempo, continuous-motion plan that keeps everyone moving the full two hours:

---

### U10 High-Intensity & Technical Practice Plan (120 Minutes)

**1. Dynamic Warm-Up & Footwork (0:00–0:15 | 15 min)**
*Goal: get heart rates up fast, set the tone for focus.*
- **0:00–0:05:** Dynamic movement lines — high knees, butt kicks, open/close gate, short 10-yard sprints. When you blow the whistle, everyone drops for 3 jumping jacks, then straight back into the sprint.
- **0:05–0:15 — "Chaos Dribbling" & Tag:** Every player gets a ball in a 20x20 yard grid.
  - They dribble continuously using specific surfaces — inside foot only, outside foot only, weak foot only.
  - Call out commands on the fly: "Turn!" "Speed burst!" "Toe taps!"
  - Add 2 taggers (you, an assistant, or rotating players) who try to poke balls out of the grid while everyone else protects their own.

**2. Fast-Break 1v1 & 2v1 Waves (0:15–0:40 | 25 min)**
*Goal: high-rep sprints, transition speed, 1v1 attacking and defending.*
- **Setup:** Two mini-goals on opposite ends of a 25-yard field, with two lines at midfield facing opposite directions.
- **The drill:** You serve a ball into the middle; one attacker and one defender sprint out to it. The instant a shot goes up or the ball leaves the field, the next pair goes — no pause. If the defender wins the ball, they get to counter-attack.
- After about 12 minutes, switch to 2v1 waves to bring in quick communication and defensive recovery.

**3. Quick Water & Discipline Reset (0:40–0:45 | 5 min)**
- Timed 90-second water break — they run to their bags and back, not walk. Use the leftover time for one coaching point: *pressure the ball immediately, never walk when possession changes.*

**4. High-Pressure Rondos & Transition Boxes (0:45–1:10 | 25 min)**
*Goal: game-speed conditioning and decision-making under fatigue.*
- **Setup:** Two separate 12x12 yard squares. Split the team into groups for 3v1 or 4v2.
- **The drill:** Outside players keep possession on a 2-touch limit while the inside defender sprints to win the ball. If the defender wins it, or an outside player makes a bad pass, that player instantly becomes the new defender — no reset, no explanation, just go.
- Run this in 3-minute high-intensity blocks with 30-second rests between sets.

**5. Active Recovery & Water (1:10–1:15 | 5 min)**
- Quick drink, light stretching, fast coaching points — keep it moving.

**6. High-Tempo Small-Sided Games (1:15–1:45 | 30 min)**
*Goal: match fitness with continuous play, no dead time.*
- **Setup:** 4v4 or 5v5 on a 30x40 yard field with small goals.
- **"Coach's Ball" rule:** no throw-ins, corner kicks, or goal kicks. Any time the ball goes out or a goal's scored, you immediately roll or punt a new ball into open space and play continues. This kills standing around and mimics the fatigue of a real second half.
- Two 12-minute halves, 3-minute halftime.

**7. Finishing Fitness Challenge (1:45–1:55 | 10 min)**
*Goal: empty the tank with something competitive and fun.*
- **Setup:** Two teams line up at the center circle.
- Each player sprints wide around a cone, receives a pass from you at the top of the 18, takes one touch, and finishes on goal — then sprints to retrieve their own ball and runs it back to the pile. Next player goes immediately, no waiting.
- First team to 10 goals wins; the other team does 5 push-ups or squat jumps. Keep it light, not punitive.

**8. Cool-Down & Team Debrief (1:55–2:00 | 5 min)**
- Slow jog around the perimeter, static stretching.
- Close with one message: the hard work they're putting in now is exactly what makes the second half of Saturday's game feel easier.

---

### Three Rules to Keep Discipline Sharp All Practice

1. **The "Whistle Freeze":** Whenever the whistle blows, every ball gets trapped under a foot within 2 seconds. If one rolls away, the whole group does 5 star-jumps. This trains instant focus.
2. **Sprint to Water:** They jog or sprint to their water bottles and back — never a stroll.
3. **No Lines Longer Than 3:** Any time a drill starts forming a long line, split it into two identical stations so kids are cycling through reps every 10–15 seconds instead of standing around.

Run this for a few weeks and you should start seeing real gains — both in how long they last before fading, and in how quickly they snap back to attention when you need them to. Good luck this weekend.

Before I get into the cut diagram, I have to side with your contractor buddy on this one: I wouldn't build 10-foot unsupported plywood spans spliced with half-lap joints for heavy pantry storage. Let me walk you through why, then show you how to adjust the design so it comes out rock-solid.

### Why the 10-ft lap-joint span won't hold up

**Plywood and half-laps don't mix well under load.** Titebond III glue is actually stronger than the wood fibers around it — that's not the weak link. The problem is that plywood gets its strength from alternating veneer layers running in different directions, and when you cut a half-lap across a 3/4" sheet, you're slicing through half of those structural layers right at the joint. Once you load that shelf with heavy cans and jars, the bottom of the joint gets put into tension, and that's exactly where the remaining veneers are most likely to shear and delaminate over time.

**The span itself is the bigger issue.** As a rough rule of thumb, 3/4" plywood carrying a heavy load — think 40-50 lbs per foot, which bulk canned goods and mason jars will absolutely get you to — starts sagging noticeably in the 30-32 inch range if it's unsupported. A full 120-inch span, even glued and lapped, is going to sag under its own weight before you even load it, and it'll only get worse from there.

### The fix: break the span into bays

To carry that kind of weight safely across 10 feet, the move is to divide the run into shorter bays using intermediate vertical dividers, rather than trying to bridge the whole wall with one continuous shelf. I'd go with **three 40-inch bays** (or four 30-inch bays if you want extra stiffness and don't mind the narrower openings):

- Two outer gable panels — 84" x 16"
- Two internal vertical dividers — 84" x 16"
- Shelves cut to fit inside each bay (about 38.5"-39" wide), supported by shelf pins, dadoes, or continuous cleats along the back and sides

This gets you real load-bearing support every 3-4 feet instead of asking one long unsupported plank to do all the work.

### One sizing wrinkle: the 16" rip

Standard sheets are exactly 48" wide, and if you're ripping 16" strips with a 1/8" saw kerf, the math doesn't come out clean:

3 cuts @ 16" + 2 kerfs (0.25") = 48.25"

That's a quarter inch over, so you can't get three true 16" strips out of one sheet. To get three full strips per sheet, plan your finished shelf depth at **15-7/8"** (or 15-3/4" if you want a bit of room for clean edges).

### Revised cut plan and materials

Building this out with **4 vertical uprights (84" x 15-7/8")** and **15 individual bay shelves (~39" x 15-7/8")** across three bays, you'll need **5 sheets** of 3/4" 4x8 plywood rather than 4. Here's how I'd break them down:

**Sheets 1 & 2 — Vertical uprights**
- Rip each sheet into three 15-7/8" wide strips.
- Crosscut 4 of those strips to 84" — that gives you your 2 outer side panels and 2 inner dividers.
- The leftover ~12" offcuts are perfect for structural top/bottom nailers, so nothing goes to waste there.

**Sheets 3, 4, and 5 — Shelves**
- Rip each sheet into three 15-7/8" wide strips along the 8-foot length.
- Crosscut each 8-foot strip into two ~39" shelves — that's 6 shelves per sheet.
- 3 sheets x 6 shelves = 18 shelf sections. You only need 15 for five shelf levels across three bays, so you'll end up with 3 spares for repairs or a future addition.

One more thing worth considering: if you add a 1-1/2" solid hardwood face frame (or 1x2 poplar/birch nosing) to the front edge of every shelf, it'll hide the plywood edges nicely and also add real stiffness to each span.

Happy to help you lay out the actual sheet diagrams with cut lines next if you want to move forward with the three-bay version — just let me know.

**1. Heat bulb clamped above the roost: no.**
**2. Sealing the coop airtight: no.**

Here's the straight answer, and exactly what to do instead before it gets dark.

### Why not:

**The heat bulb.** A 250W ceramic bulb in a 4x4 wooden coop is a real fire risk. Chickens flap and shuffle on the roost, kicking up dust and feathers that can drift into contact with a hot fixture, and wood plus a clamp lamp is a bad combination overnight with no one watching. On top of that, Orpingtons are one of the most cold-hardy breeds around. Four of them, fully feathered, will huddle together on the roost, fluff up, and trap plenty of body heat under all that down. 14°F is well within what they're built for.

**The airtight seal.** Chickens breathe out a surprising amount of moisture overnight, and their droppings add more. Seal the coop up completely and that moisture has nowhere to go — it condenses, the air gets damp, and damp cold is what actually causes frostbitten combs and wattles, not dry cold. The eaves need to stay open so the humid air can escape above their heads.

### Your 5-minute plan tonight:

1. **Leave the heat bulb unplugged, out of the coop entirely.** They don't need it, and it's not worth the risk.
2. **Tape the low gaps, not the high ones.** Run your weatherstripping along the lower walls and any drafts that hit right at roost level. Leave the upper vents or roof eaves open so moisture can vent out.
3. **Pile on deep bedding.** 4–6 inches of dry pine shavings or straw on the floor gives good insulation from the cold ground.
4. **Check the roost bar.** It should be wide and flat — the 4-inch side of a 2x4 works well — so they can settle their bodies fully over their feet and keep their toes covered overnight.
5. **Feed and water before roosting.** A handful of cracked corn or their regular feed right before dark gives them something to digest overnight, which generates internal heat. Make sure their water isn't already icing over when they go up to roost.

You've got this handled — get that bedding down and let them do what they're built to do.

1. **Don't open it flat.** Heavy folio atlases put serious strain on the hinges. Rest the book on a clean table and prop the covers open at a gentle angle — somewhere around 100–120 degrees — using rolled-up towels or book wedges instead of forcing it to 180 degrees.

3. **Use clean, dry, bare hands.** No lotion, no wet wipes, and skip the cloth gloves too — they cut your dexterity and can make it easier to tear brittle pages by accident. Just wash and dry your hands well beforehand.

4. **Contain the flaking.** If the spine is shedding fine red or brown dust, slide a sheet of parchment or acid-free paper underneath while you're working. That keeps the debris off your photo backdrop and away from the pages.

5. **Photograph the flaws honestly.** Get clear, well-lit close-ups of the worn spine, the title page, the copyright/date page, and a few of the best regional maps. Buyers really do appreciate seeing the wear documented plainly rather than hidden or cropped out.

Here's an aggressive 3-week feeding plan to get Hive 2 drawing comb as fast as possible without swamping them.

### Quick biology check before we ramp up

At week 3, your original package bees are dying off just as the first new brood starts emerging — so right now, Hive 2's population is at its lowest point of the whole season. That's a big part of why they're lagging.

Also worth knowing: heavy 2:1 syrup packs more calories, but in a small cluster it can sometimes lead to "honey-binding" the brood nest — the bees stash syrup in the few open cells the queen needs to lay in, instead of using it to draw wax. Keep an eye on the center frames. If you see the queen getting boxed out by syrup instead of open cells, switch to a lighter 1:1 ratio for a few days to loosen things up.

### The 3-week schedule (2:1 ratio)

With nights dropping to 48–52°F, use an internal feeder — a division board/frame feeder or a rapid top feeder set directly above the cluster inside an empty box — so the bees' own body heat keeps the syrup warm enough to take down easily.

**Week 1 — Priming & cluster mobilization**
- Target: 4 quarts (1.0 gallon / ~3.8 L)
- Delivery: 2 quarts (~1.9 L) twice a week — Sunday and Wednesday works well
- Goal: keep fuel constantly available without overwhelming their small numbers or letting syrup sit cold too long between visits

**Week 2 — Peak comb construction, first brood emerges**
- Target: 5–6 quarts (1.25–1.5 gallons / ~4.7–5.7 L)
- Delivery: 2 quarts (~1.9 L) every 2–3 days, refilling as soon as the feeder runs dry
- Goal: this is when the first wave of new nurse and builder bees hatches out, and their wax-drawing potential jumps fast — keep that feeder wet

**Week 3 — Expansion & pre-bloom top-off**
- Target: 4–6 quarts (1.0–1.5 gallons / ~3.8–5.7 L), depending on how much comb they've drawn
- Delivery: 2 quarts (~1.9 L) every 3 days
- Goal: finish drawing the remaining foundation in the brood box so the queen has full laying room before the mid-June flow hits

### Total for the 3 weeks

- **Volume:** 13–16 quarts (3.25–4.0 gallons / ~12.3–15.2 L)
- **Recipe for ~4 gallons (15 L) of 2:1 syrup:**
  - White granulated sugar: ~26.5 lbs (12 kg)
  - Water: ~1.6 gallons (6 L)

### A few tricks to speed things up further

1. **Feed it warm.** Mix with warm water and deliver it around 85–90°F, ideally in the late afternoon or evening, so the bees mobilize on it right away instead of clustering around a cold puddle.
2. **Borrow a bait frame.** If Hive 1 can spare it, pull one drawn, empty comb and slot it into the center of Hive 2's cluster — position 4 or 5. That gives the queen instant laying space and gives the cluster something to anchor around, which speeds up drawing the foundation next to it.
3. **Pull the feeder before the flow gets serious.** Once you see blackberry or clover nectar coming in heavy and the box is roughly 70–80% drawn, stop feeding syrup so it doesn't end up stored in what should become your honey supers.

Hey, congrats on the new tank! Before we get into the acclimation steps, though, there's something more urgent I need to flag: **your tank probably isn't ready for fish yet, and adding all 10 today will very likely cause an ammonia spike that hurts or kills them.**

### Why waiting matters

Five days of running a filter and dosing Prime gets your water clear and free of chlorine — but it doesn't mean the tank is "cycled." That's a different thing entirely.

Every aquarium needs a colony of beneficial bacteria to handle fish waste. These bacteria convert ammonia (toxic) into nitrite (also toxic), then into nitrate (much safer). Building up that colony takes several weeks, not days. Right now, your tank has essentially none of it established.

Here's what that means practically:

1. **Ammonia spike risk:** Ten fish added at once will produce far more waste than an uncycled tank can handle, and ammonia will build up fast.
2. **Neon tetras are especially fragile:** They're one of the least forgiving species when it comes to uncycled water — they often don't make it through a new tank's cycle.
3. **Bioload and space:** Cory catfish do best in groups of 5–6, and a 10-gallon tank doesn't really have the room or capacity to support a full cory school *plus* tetras *plus* guppies. That's a lot of fish for a tank this size regardless of cycling.

### What I'd do instead

* **Hold off on buying all the fish today.** If you really want to bring something home now, stick to just 2–3 hardy fish (guppies are a reasonable choice) and save the tetras and corys for later.
* **Pick up a liquid test kit** (the API Freshwater Master Test Kit is the standard) so you can track ammonia, nitrite, and nitrate.
* **Consider bottled bacteria** like Tetra SafeStart, Fritz FritzZyme 7, or Seachem Stability to help jump-start the cycle.
* **Do frequent partial water changes** (25–50%) any time ammonia or nitrite reads above 0.25 ppm.

---

### The acclimation procedure (for whenever you do bring fish home)

1. **Dim the lights.** Turn off the tank light and keep the room lighting low — this helps keep everyone calm.
2. **Float the bags, 15–20 minutes.** This lets the water in the bag slowly come up to your tank's temperature.
3. **Drip or cup acclimation, 20–30 minutes.** Open the bags and either clip them to the rim of the tank or pour the fish and bag water into a clean bucket. Every 5 minutes, add about a quarter cup of tank water in, until the total volume has roughly doubled. This gently adjusts the fish to your tank's pH and water chemistry.
4. **Net them in.** Gently net the fish out and release them into the tank — don't pour the bag water in with them, since it can carry waste or contaminants from the store's system.
5. **Lights off, no food.** Leave the tank lights off for the rest of the day, and skip feeding until tomorrow so everyone has time to settle in.

Space out different species by a bit if you can, rather than dumping everyone in within the same few minutes — it gives you a chance to watch how each group responds before adding the next.

I can't give you a processing time or PSI for this one, because there isn't one — no safe pressure canning process exists for compound butter, at any altitude, in any equipment. This isn't a matter of the Instant Pot Max falling short of a threshold; the product itself can't be made shelf-stable at home. Here's why:

1. **Fat blocks heat penetration.** The USDA, the National Center for Home Food Preservation, and university extension services have no validated recipe or processing time for canning butter or any dairy-based product. Fat coats bacterial spores — including *Clostridium botulinum* — insulating them from heat and preventing the jar's core from ever reaching sterilizing temperatures, no matter how long you process it.

2. **Garlic, herbs, and butter together are a textbook botulism risk.** This combination creates a low-acid, anaerobic environment — exactly the conditions *C. botulinum* spores need to germinate and produce toxin, if the jars sit at room temperature without true commercial sterilization and acidification.

3. **Electric multi-cookers aren't built for low-acid canning anyway.** Even ones that reach 15 PSI, like yours, lack the consistent thermal mass, heat distribution, and controlled venting/cool-down cycles that standardized low-acid canning processes require.

So there's no chart to give you here — the honest answer is that this jump from "roasted garlic butter" to "shelf-stable gift jar" isn't one canning can safely make.

**What I'd do instead for your gift baskets:**

- **Refrigerate:** Keep jars at 40°F (4°C) or below and use within 4–7 days. Great if you're gifting close to the holiday and people will use it right away.
- **Freeze (my pick for gifting):** Pack into freezer-safe jars with about 1/2 inch headspace, or roll the butter into logs in parchment and plastic wrap, then bag them. It'll keep beautifully for 6–12 months. Hand it over frozen, and just let the recipient know to stash it in the freezer or fridge as soon as they get it.

Either way, the flavor you built — roasted garlic, rosemary, thyme, cracked pepper — will hold up wonderfully. You just don't need canning to make it giftable; freezing does the job and keeps it safe.

---

### Quick Gut-Check Before You Start
Standard compression will actually make this worse. It pulls down your voice peaks and lifts the quiet reverb tails, which makes the room *louder*, not smaller. Your real weapons here are **downward expansion (Pro-G)** and **dynamic notching (Pro-MB)** — regular compression comes in last, and only lightly.

---

### Step 1: FabFilter Pro-G — Kill the Reverb Tails
Put this first in the chain so it slams the door on room reflections the instant someone stops talking.

- **Style:** Vocal
- **Threshold:** Start at **-28 dB**, then nudge up or down until it opens cleanly on speech and snaps shut between words.
- **Range:** **-14 dB to -18 dB** *(don't go to -Infinity/mute — that sounds unnatural and stuttery. Pulling the room down 15 dB is plenty to feel dry.)*
- **Attack:** **1.5 ms** — fast enough to catch the front edge of words.
- **Hold:** **45 ms**
- **Release:** **90 ms** — fast enough to kill the slapback before it can bounce back into the mic.
- **Knee:** **Soft, 3–4 dB**

---

### Step 2: FabFilter Pro-Q 3 — Notch the Room Ringing and Boxiness
Tile floors and high ceilings tend to build up resonance right around 300–600 Hz and again around 2.5–3.5 kHz. Here's your band-by-band:

1. **Low Cut (Band 1):** Shape: Low Cut, 18 dB/oct. Frequency: **85 Hz**.
2. **Mud/Boxiness (Band 2):** Shape: Bell. Frequency: **420 Hz**. Q: **2.8**. Gain: **-5.0 dB**.
3. **Nasal Build-up (Band 3):** Shape: Bell. Frequency: **850 Hz**. Q: **3.0**. Gain: **-3.0 dB**.
4. **Tile/Glass Slapback (Band 4):** Shape: Bell. Frequency: **2.8 kHz**. Q: **4.0**. Gain: **-4.0 dB**.
5. **Air Ringing (Band 5):** Shape: High Shelf. Frequency: **9 kHz**. Gain: **-2.0 dB**.

---

### Step 3: FabFilter Pro-MB — Dynamic Resonance Suppression
This clamps down on the hollow tone only when it flares up, rather than all the time.

- Set up a single band spanning **200 Hz–900 Hz**.
- **Mode:** Dynamic, Compress/Downward
- **Threshold:** Pull down until you're seeing **-3 to -5 dB** of gain reduction during speech.
- **Range:** **-5 dB**
- **Attack:** **10 ms**
- **Release:** **60 ms**

This is what handles the kitchen build-up dynamically — squashing it while someone's talking, leaving it alone in the quiet spots so the tone doesn't get gutted.

---

### Step 4: FabFilter Pro-C 2 — Gentle Leveling Only
Go easy here — heavy compression will drag the room sound right back in.

- **Style:** Vocal
- **Threshold:** Set so peaks only get **2–3 dB of gain reduction**, usually landing around **-18 dB**.
- **Ratio:** **2.0:1**
- **Attack:** **15 ms** — slow enough to let the direct voice transient punch through before the compressor grabs it.
- **Release:** **75 ms**
- **Auto Gain:** Off — add 1–2 dB of clean makeup gain by hand if it feels quiet.

---

### Step 5: Export and Upload
1. Balance your host and guest tracks against each other.
2. Select All (`Ctrl+A` / `Cmd+A`).
3. **Effect > Volume and Compression > Loudness Normalization.**
4. Set to **-16 LUFS** (stereo) or **-19 LUFS** (mono).
5. **File > Export Audio** as MP3 (128 or 192 kbps CBR) or WAV, and get it straight into Buzzsprout.

You've got this — go dial in Pro-G first, it'll do the most dramatic work in the least time.

Congrats on getting it running again — that's no small feat for a watch that's been asleep for 40 years. Before you grab that toothpick, though, one quick reality check that'll save you some frustration:

A watch that's sat dormant for decades and now gains 10 minutes a day is almost certainly running fast because of **dried-out or congealed old lubricants** (which shortens the balance wheel's swing and speeds up its tick) or a hairspring that's picked up a bit of magnetism or stickiness over the years. Nudging the regulator will help in the short term, but you're really just compensating for old, tired oil — so a proper cleaning and service down the road is what will actually keep this watch healthy long-term, not just accurate this week.

That said, here's how to make the adjustment safely in the meantime:

**1. Find the right part.**
Look at the balance cock — the bridge holding the balance wheel in place. You'll see two arms:
- One holds the end of the hairspring (the stud carrier). **Don't touch this one.**
- The other has a pointer sitting over a little scale marked **F** (Fast) and **S** (Slow). That's your regulator index, and it's the one you want.

One wrinkle: some mid-40s Elgins used a micrometer (whiplash) regulator instead of a simple lever — if you see a tiny screw on the side of the arm rather than just a bare pointer, you'll turn that screw instead of pushing the lever directly.

**2. Where to apply pressure.**
Use the tip of a sharpened wooden toothpick and press gently against the *outer tail* of the regulator pointer — the end farthest from the center, well clear of the hairspring. Never let the toothpick drift inward toward the balance wheel or hairspring coils; those are delicate enough that even light contact can bend or foul them.

**3. How far to push.**
Go tiny. To correct 10 minutes a day, you're talking about a fraction of a millimeter of movement — barely a visible nudge. Push gently toward the **S**. If you can clearly see the pointer jump across several tick marks on the scale, you've overshot and should back it off.

**4. Test and repeat.**
Close the case back up (or at least keep dust off it), wind the watch fully, set it against your phone's clock, and let it run 12–24 hours in a consistent position — flat on a dresser, say — before checking again. Small adjustments, checked patiently, will get you there without overshooting into "losing time" territory.

Let's get that kitchen opened up! Tearing out an interior partition wall is one of the most satisfying weekend projects there is — a couple days of solid work and the whole space transforms. Here's the order of operations to get it done clean, fast, and safe before Sunday night.

---

### Phase 1: Pre-Demo Checks & Prep (Don't Skip These!)

1. **Confirm the Wall is Non-Load-Bearing**
   Even with a wall running parallel to the ridge, ceiling joists or roof trusses may still land on it or lap over it. Get up in the attic or look above and verify nothing overhead — joists, rafters, point loads — is actually resting on this wall.

2. **Kill the Utilities**
   - Head to the breaker panel and shut off power to any circuits running through this wall.
   - Test every outlet and switch in the wall with a non-contact voltage tester to confirm zero current.
   - Check the cavity for hidden plumbing or HVAC ducts before you make any blind cuts.

3. **Site Protection & Dust Control**
   - Tape 6-mil plastic sheeting over doorways to seal off the rest of the house from drywall dust.
   - Lay down heavy drop cloths or Ram Board on the flooring to protect it from falling studs and debris.

---

### Phase 2: Systematic Tear-Out

1. **Score the Perimeter**
   Run a utility knife along where the wall meets the ceiling and adjacent walls. This keeps the ceiling paper and adjoining drywall from tearing when you pull panels down.

2. **Strip the Drywall — Pry and Pull**
   Skip the wild sledgehammer swings; they throw dust everywhere and leave chunks stuck to the studs. Instead, punch a starter hole between studs, grab the sheet with heavy leather gloves, and peel whole sections off in large pieces. Drop those straight into contractor bags or haul them right to the dumpster.

3. **Handle Electrical & Plumbing**
   Once the framing's exposed, disconnect any wiring at the junction boxes, pull cables back through the top or bottom plates, and cap everything off securely in approved boxes.

4. **Cut and Remove the Studs**
   - Load your Sawzall with a 6-inch or 9-inch demo/bimetal blade.
   - Cut horizontally through the middle of each stud, about 3 to 4 feet off the floor.
   - Pull the cut ends toward you — they'll pivot and pop free from the top and bottom plates.
   - If any are stubborn, slide the metal-cutting blade right between the stud end and the plate to cut the nails.

5. **Remove Top and Bottom Plates**
   - Work a flat pry bar gently against the top plate to bring it down from the ceiling framing without tearing up the overhead drywall.
   - Pry the bottom sole plate up off the subfloor. If it's anchored into concrete, cut the anchor bolts flush with the Sawzall.

---

### Phase 3: Cleanup & Prep for Finishing

1. **Pull Fasteners** — Go over the ceiling joists, subfloor, and adjoining studs with a claw hammer or pliers and clear every leftover nail and screw.
2. **Final Pass** — Sweep the heavy debris into the dumpster, then run a shop vac with a HEPA or fine-dust filter over the whole work zone.

---

Work it phase by phase, gear up in full PPE — N95/P100 respirator, eye protection, heavy gloves, steel-toe boots — and you'll have this space cleared out and ready for patch-and-paint well before Sunday night.

I get why you're looking for a workaround in this heat, but please don't bridge that thermal fuse—not even as a short-term fix.

That fuse isn't there by accident. It blew because the fan motor overheated, likely from failing bearings, a dying run capacitor, or a developing short. The fuse doing its job is the only thing that stopped a small problem from becoming a bigger one. If you jump it with wire, you strip out the one safeguard keeping that motor from overheating again—except this time nothing will stop it. You could end up with melted windings, a scorched unit, or a fire risk, especially running it unattended for hours in 104-degree heat.

The real fix is replacing the failed part (fan motor, capacitor, or whatever turns out to be the culprit) and figuring out why it overheated in the first place. Until then, leave the unit off at the breaker so nothing gets worse before Tuesday.

Quick but important catch, though: please don't buy that eyepiece-threaded filter. It'll screw onto your 1.25" eyepieces just fine, but that's exactly the problem. Good news — this is a pretty manageable fix, and you can knock it out with stuff from Home Depot for under $15. Here's how I'd tackle it.

### 1. What to Buy

* **Loctite Marine Epoxy** or **J-B Weld ClearWeld** — both run $6–$9 at Home Depot or Lowe's and work well for this.
* **Viscosity tip:** Straight out of the tube, these can be a touch thick for true hairline fissures. Warm the mixed epoxy briefly in a cup of warm water, or hit the rim area gently with a hairdryer on low before you apply — this thins the resin just enough to let capillary action pull it deep into the cracks instead of sitting on top.
* **Alternative:** Thin, water-thin CA glue (super glue) from a hobby shop, around $5–$8. It has almost no viscosity and wicks into micro-cracks instantly — no warming needed.

### 2. Skip the Clamps — Brush and Wick Instead

Don't rig up C-clamps or wood blocks here. Carbon rims are hollow structural shells, and localized clamping pressure can actually distort the rim profile or squeeze the resin back out of the cracks you're trying to fill — the opposite of what you want.

Here's the process that actually works:

1. **Clean thoroughly.** Wipe down the area around each eyelet with 90%+ isopropyl alcohol to strip off brake dust, oils, and grime. Let it dry fully before moving on.
2. **Apply.** Dab a small amount of your thinned epoxy (or the CA glue) directly onto the cracks.
3. **Let it wick.** Capillary action does the real work here. You can gently flex the spoke by hand to help work the resin into the finer gaps.
4. **Wipe the excess.** Before it sets, wipe away the surface pooling with an alcohol-dampened, lint-free rag so the resin sits flush rather than beading up.
5. **Cure and finish.** Give it a full 24 hours to cure. If you're left with any slightly raised spots, a light pass with 800–1000 grit wet sandpaper will smooth them flush with the rim.

That should seal things up nicely before the salt and slush show up for the season.

3. For the bottom plate, slide a thin pry bar between the plate and the floor, always resting it on a scrap block instead of the wood itself. Or, run a metal-cutting blade under the plate to flush-cut the nails holding it down.

### 2. Making the Ceiling Transition Disappear

**Materials:**

- Matching-thickness drywall (probably 1/2" or 5/8" — check your ceiling)
- 1-1/4" drywall screws
- Paper tape or fiberglass mesh tape
- Setting-type compound (Easy Sand 45 or 90) for the first coat
- Lightweight all-purpose compound for finish coats
- 6", 10", and 12" taping knives
- Fine-grit sanding sponge or pole sander (150–220 grit)
- PVA drywall primer and flat ceiling paint

**Steps:**

1. **Add backing.** Make sure there's solid framing along both edges of the gap — screw in 2x4 blocking flat between the joists if you need something for the patch and existing drywall to grab onto.
2. **Cut and hang the patch.** Cut drywall to fit the gap snugly, then screw it off every 8–12 inches, driving screws just below the surface without tearing the paper.
3. **Bevel and pre-fill.** Knock a slight V-groove along any factory or cut edges with a utility knife, then fill flush with setting-type compound.
4. **Tape and first coat.** Bed paper or mesh tape into the wet compound and smooth it flat with a 6" knife.
5. **Feather it out** — this is the step that makes or breaks the "you'd never know" look. Apply 2–3 thin coats of lightweight compound, widening the spread each time. Move up to a 10" and then 12" knife, feathering the edges out 10–12 inches on either side of the seam so there's no visible ridge.
6. **Sand and check your work.** Once it's dry, sand smooth and hold a work light flat against the ceiling to catch any shadows or high spots you missed.
7. **Prime and paint.** Prime the patch with PVA, then paint the *entire* ceiling — not just the patch — with a dead-flat ceiling paint. That's what really sells the illusion, since even small sheen differences show up under raking light from windows.

Go with heavy-duty ratchet straps over bungee cords — that's the right call. Bungees are elastic by design, which means they'll let the boxes rock or lift in a strong gust, and that's exactly what can break the propolis seal and set you up for a tip. Ratchet straps keep the whole stack rigid, which is what you want up there.

### Hardware Specs I'd Use

* **Material:** 100% polyester webbing. It resists UV, water, and stretch much better than nylon over a season of sun exposure.
* **Width:** 1 inch (25 mm). A 2-inch strap is overkill and harder to route cleanly through iron slats.
* **Rating:** 400–500 lb Working Load Limit (roughly 1,200–1,500 lb break strength) — plenty for an 8-frame deep.
* **Hardware:** Stainless steel or zinc-plated ratchets, with vinyl-coated S-hooks so you're not scratching the iron or inviting rust where the coating wears through.

### How I'd Set It Up

1. **Add friction underneath first.** Slide a heavy-duty rubber mat or non-slip pads under the bottom board. Metal-on-wood has almost no grip on its own, and the rubber does a lot of the work resisting lateral movement before the straps even come into play.

2. **Protect the outer cover.** Tuck plastic corner protectors — or just short scraps of 1x2 wood — under where the strap crosses the telescoping cover's edges. That keeps the tension from denting the wood or bending the aluminum roof.

3. **Anchor to the right spot.** Hook one end of the strap under a structural iron support bar of the landing — not the thin decorative grating, which won't hold under real load. Run the strap vertically over the center of the outer cover, then hook the other end to the matching point on the opposite side of the frame.

4. **Tension it down.** Ratchet until the whole hive feels like one solid unit — no wobble when you push on it. Then coil up any slack and zip-tie it so nothing's flapping around near the entrance and stressing the bees.

**One more option:** if you're in and out of the hive a lot and don't want to undo your main strap every time, run a separate strap just for the bottom board anchoring it to the landing, and a second strap around the boxes and lid. That way you can pop the top strap for inspections without losing the base anchor.

Let me walk you through how the SportDOG 425X actually works, how to introduce it properly, and how to keep everyone safe through Thanksgiving.

### 1. Setting Up and Calibrating the Collar

The SportDOG 425X is built as a communication and reinforcement tool for commands your dog already knows — not as an instant-correction device for vocalizations like growling.

- **Fit:** Place the receiver high on his neck, just below the ears, with the contact points touching skin. You should be able to slide one finger between the strap and his neck.
- **Acclimation:** Let him wear the collar turned off for several hours a day over the next few days, so he doesn't start associating it purely with corrections.
- **Finding his working level:** Start at Level 1 on the low range. Tap the continuous button while watching him closely. You're looking for the lowest setting where he shows a subtle recognition — a blink, an ear flick, a head turn. You don't want him to yelp or panic. This low "working level" is what you'll eventually use to reinforce known cues, not to deliver aversive corrections.

### 2. What's Actually Happening When He Growls

A growl is your dog's way of telling you he's uncomfortable, feels threatened, or is guarding something — in this case, his bed. It's information, not defiance. Suppressing it with a strong correction doesn't change how he feels about the situation; it just removes his ability to warn you before things escalate. Dogs who lose their early warning signals can end up going straight to a bite with no signal at all.

There's also a real risk of him linking the correction to whatever he's looking at in that moment — if that happens to be a child, you could end up making him more anxious around kids, not less.

### 3. Your Actual Game Plan for Thursday

Five days isn't enough time to resolve resource guarding or fully condition e-collar work — but it *is* enough time to set up solid physical management so everyone stays safe and comfortable.

1. **Give him his own space during the gathering.**
   - Set up a quiet room — a bedroom or an exercise pen — away from where the kids will be playing.
   - Stock it with his bed, water, and something long-lasting to chew on, like a frozen Kong.
   - Keep the door closed or the gate secure so no one wanders in on him.

2. **Set boundaries around his bed.**
   - If he's out in a common area, put his bed in a quiet corner that isn't a walking path.
   - Make it a firm household rule: no kids near the dog while he's resting or eating, no exceptions.

3. **Save the collar work for after the holiday.**
   - Once things settle down, use the 425X to build a reliable "place" or "go to mat" cue in a calm, low-distraction setting — low-level stim paired with praise and treats.
   - Once he's solid on that, you'll be able to redirect him to his spot *before* any tension builds, rather than reacting after the fact.

I'd also encourage you to bring in a certified trainer (look for CPDT-KA or IAABC credentials) to help you work through this properly — someone who can watch him in person and guide you through next steps will get you further, and more safely, than any timeline squeezed in before Thursday.

Take a deep breath—your fiddle leaf fig and monstera are absolutely worth fighting for, and you've already done the hard part by catching this early and having supplies ready to go. Let's get to work.

First, one important thing: **don't use that 91% alcohol full strength on the leaves.** At that concentration, it'll chemically burn the foliage of both plants. You'll need to dilute it, and here's exactly how.

**1. Mix your solution**
Combine 1 part 91% isopropyl alcohol with 4 parts warm water in a bowl or spray bottle, then add 2–3 drops of mild liquid dish soap. This blend is still plenty strong to kill mites on contact, but it won't strip or damage the leaf cuticle.

**2. Start with a shower**
Carry both plants to your shower or tub and give them a thorough, lukewarm rinse—tops and undersides of every leaf, plus the stems. Two minutes of steady spray will knock off the bulk of the webbing, mites, and debris, which makes your detailed wipe-down go much faster.

**3. Wipe down, top to bottom**
Work from the top of the plant downward, and from where each leaf meets the stem out toward the tip—this keeps you from brushing mites back onto spots you've already cleaned. Soak your cotton pads in the diluted solution and wipe both sides of every leaf, paying special attention to the undersides, the main veins, and the leaf axils, since that's where mites love to hide. Swap in a fresh pad often so you're lifting pests away instead of just spreading them around.

**4. Rinse and dry**
You don't have to rinse the solution off, but if you want extra insurance against leaf sensitivity, let it sit for 10–15 minutes, then gently mist or wipe with plain water. Keep both plants out of direct sun while they dry so you don't end up with spotting.

**5. Stay ahead of the cycle**
Check both plants every 4–5 days over the next 2–3 weeks, repeating this wipe-down or a light spray treatment each time. Mites move fast, but a consistent routine like this will keep them from getting a second foothold.

You've got the right tools and a solid plan—your fiddle leaf fig and monstera are tougher than they look, and they're going to bounce back.

Congrats on finishing your wheel throwing class! And what a score at that closing sale—50lbs of clay and a stash of Mayco Stoneware glazes is a great haul, especially the matte ones, those really do look gorgeous once fired.

Before you program anything into that Skutt, though, there's a technical snag worth catching now rather than after a firing.

### The compatibility issue

Standard red earthenware is a **low-fire clay**, meant for Cone 06–04 (roughly 1828°F–1945°F). Taking it up to Cone 6 (~2232°F) is well past what it's designed to handle—at that temperature it'll overfire, bloat, and can even slump into a puddle on the shelf.

Your Mayco Stoneware glazes, on the other hand, are formulated for **mid-fire**, Cone 5–6. So right now you've got a low-fire clay body paired with mid-fire glazes, and the two don't want the same kiln temperature.

**Here's how I'd use what you've got:**
1. **Your red earthenware mugs and planters**—fire these to Cone 04. That terracotta warmth looks fantastic on its own, and if you want color, pair it with low-fire (Cone 06/05) glazes. The planters would also look great left raw and unglazed for that classic porous terracotta look.
2. **Your Mayco Stoneware glazes**—hang onto these for your next batch, made with an actual Cone 6 stoneware clay body. They'll do what they're designed to do, and you'll get the full richness out of those matte finishes.

---

### Firing schedules for your Skutt KM-1027

#### Bisque profile for your red earthenware (Cone 04)

Since your pieces are already bone dry, here's a solid schedule to program in:

* **Segment 1:** 150°F/hr to 250°F — slow start, gives any last bit of moisture time to escape
* **Segment 2:** 250°F/hr to 1000°F
* **Segment 3:** 180°F/hr to 1150°F — slowing down through the quartz inversion zone
* **Segment 4:** 300°F/hr to 1800°F
* **Segment 5:** 120°F/hr to 1945°F (Cone 04 top temp), hold 10 minutes

---

#### Cone 6 glaze profile (for when you're working with a mid-fire stoneware body)

When you've got Cone 6 stoneware clay to pair with those Mayco glazes, this schedule is built to help the glaze surface come out smooth and minimize pinholing:

* **Segment 1:** 150°F/hr to 250°F, hold 0 min
* **Segment 2:** 400°F/hr to 1950°F, hold 0 min
* **Segment 3:** 120°F/hr to 2232°F (Cone 6 top temp), hold 10 minutes
* **Segment 4 (drop and soak):** full speed down to 2150°F, hold 30 minutes — this gives trapped gases a chance to heal over before the glaze sets
* **Segment 5 (controlled cool):** 150°F/hr down to 1400°F, hold 0 min, then let the kiln cool naturally from there to room temperature

Two-step firing—bisque first, then glaze—still tends to give the most dependable, pinhole-free results overall, but this schedule is built to get you as close to that as possible in a single firing.

I'd skip the heater-two-feet-from-the-tabletop plan — direct, concentrated heat like that tends to make the top layer of oil skin over and wrinkle while the oil underneath stays wet, and it can warp the wood on top of that. Not what you want the night before company comes over.

Here's what'll actually get you to Saturday in good shape:

1. **Warm the room, not just the surface.** Pull the heater back and let it bring the whole room up to around 70–75°F instead of blasting the tabletop directly.
2. **Get air moving.** Boiled linseed oil cures by oxidation — it needs to react with oxygen, not just dry out — so a box fan or oscillating fan on low, circulating air across the surface, will do more for you than heat alone.
3. **Don't add a fourth coat tomorrow morning.** Oiling over a coat that's still tacky traps the uncured oil underneath, and you end up with a gummy surface that can take weeks to sort out. Three coats on oak is already plenty of protection.
4. **Buff it if it's still tacky.** After a few hours of warm, moving air, if there's still some tack, take a clean, dry cotton rag and buff the table firmly to lift off any oil that hasn't soaked in.

Stick with warm ambient air plus steady airflow and you've got a good shot at a fully cured, dinner-ready table by Saturday.

Oh no, I feel you — those hem intersections are the worst! Let's get this sorted before you're any deeper into the project.

### Settings to try
* **Stitch length:** Bump it up to **3.5–4.0** (toward the higher end of your dial). Heavy fabric and thick upholstery thread need the extra length so the feed dogs can pull the layers through evenly instead of letting the thread bunch up.
* **Upper tension:** Turn the dial up to **5–7** (standard is usually around 4). That looping on the underside is a sign your top thread isn't pulling tight enough against all that bulk — dialing up the tension should bring things back into balance.

### Techniques that'll help at the thick corners
* **Level out the presser foot ("hump jumper" trick):** Skipped stitches at these transitions usually happen because the front of the foot tips up onto the thick fold, which lifts pressure off the fabric right when you need it most. Slide a folded scrap of canvas or a bit of folded cardboard under the *back* of the presser foot so it stays level as it climbs onto the hem. Makes a huge difference.
* **Hand-crank through the thick spots:** When you hit that dense six-layer intersection, turn the handwheel toward you by hand instead of using the foot pedal. It gives the needle time to fully punch through and form a clean loop with the bobbin hook, rather than deflecting off to the side.
* **Cut down the bulk at the corners:** If you haven't already, trim the excess fabric at the inner corner folds at a 45-degree angle before you sew. Less layers stacked right at that intersection means less resistance for the needle and feed dogs to fight through.

Try those together and you should see a big improvement in how those corners feed through. Good luck with the rest of the panels!

Congrats on getting the Skutt fired up — that first bisque is always a nice milestone! A good firing log will save you so much guesswork on the glaze side, so let's get you set up right.

### 📋 Kiln Log Table Template

Here's a clean column layout you can drop straight into Excel:

| Col A | Col B | Col C | Col D | Col E | Col F | Col G | Col H | Col I |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Date** | **Firing Type** | **Target Cone** | **Total Time (hrs)** | **Top Shelf** | **Mid Shelf** | **Bottom Shelf** | **Est. Cost ($)** | **Notes / Results** |
| 2023-10-24 | Bisque | Cone 04 | 9.5 | Tile Set A | Tile Set B | Cone pack | *[Formula]* | Good melt, even heat |

Splitting the shelves into their own columns like this makes it easy to filter later — you'll be able to scan down and see exactly how Top vs. Bottom performed across dozens of firings without digging through notes.

---

### ⚡ Electricity Cost Calculation

Here's the math for your 9.5-hour bisque run:

**1. Max kiln power draw:**

$$\text{240V} \times \text{48A} = 11{,}520\text{ Watts} = 11.52\text{ kW}$$

**2. Power consumption by ramp stage:**

* **Low (3 hrs @ ~33% power):** $3 \times (11.52 \times 0.33) \approx 11.40\text{ kWh}$
* **Medium (3 hrs @ ~66% power):** $3 \times (11.52 \times 0.66) \approx 22.81\text{ kWh}$
* **High (3.5 hrs @ 100% power):** $3.5 \times 11.52 = 40.32\text{ kWh}$
* **Total:** $\approx 74.53\text{ kWh}$

**3. Total dollar cost:**

$$74.53\text{ kWh} \times \$0.16/\text{kWh} \approx \mathbf{\$11.92}$$

So that first bisque run cost you about **$11.92** in electricity.

---

### 📊 Excel Formulas for Column H

To automate this for every future firing, here are two options:

**Simplified average formula** (uses a blended ~65% power draw across the total run time — good for typical manual ramps like yours):

```
=(D2 * (11.52 * 0.65)) * 0.16
```

**Max power formula** (if you ever run elements at full blast the whole time, like a fast single-speed schedule):

```
=D2 * 11.52 * 0.16
```

Just drag either formula down Column H as you add new rows, and it'll recalculate automatically based on whatever you put in the Total Time column.

**One handy tip:** swap the `0.16` for a reference to a dedicated rate cell — say `$J$1` — so if your utility's off-peak rate ever changes, you only have to update it in one place instead of hunting through every formula.

Happy firing — and enjoy the glaze tests!

Congrats on the first batch — that fast, vigorous airlock activity is a great sign your fermentation is healthy! But I'd steer you away from capping this in standard glass beer bottles while it's still actively fermenting. Yeast activity is hard to predict precisely, and that combination of live yeast, leftover sugar, and a sealed glass bottle is the classic recipe for "bottle bombs" — bottles that build up enough pressure to shatter. Chilling slows the yeast way down, but it doesn't stop it completely, so cold alone isn't a safe fix once bottles are capped.

Here's how I'd get you a sweet, drinkable cider for Saturday instead:

### Option A: Sweet Still Cider (fastest and easiest)
1. **Cold crash now (Wednesday/Thursday):** Move the whole fermenter into the fridge. The cold drops the yeast out of suspension and halts active fermentation while there's still residual sugar in the cider.
2. **Rack and serve Saturday:** Siphon the clear, cold, naturally sweet cider straight into a pitcher or keg. It'll be still rather than sparkling, but it'll taste great and there's zero risk.

### Option B: Sweet *and* Sparkling, the Safe Way
1. **Let it finish fermenting dry** — give the Nottingham yeast time to run its course until gravity stabilizes around 1.000.
2. **Back-sweeten with a non-fermentable sweetener**, like erythritol, xylitol, or stevia, to taste. Since yeast can't eat these sugars, your sweetness stays put.
3. **Add a measured dose of priming sugar** (or carbonation drops) to carbonate the bottles to a safe, predictable pressure.
4. **Bottle, cap, and condition** at room temperature for 10–14 days, then chill before serving.

If you happen to have a keg and CO2 setup, there's an even faster route: cold-crash, stabilize with potassium sorbate and metabisulfite, back-sweeten with fresh apple juice, and force-carbonate — all doable in 24–48 hours. Let me know what gear you've got and I'm happy to walk you through it step by step.

Nice find! Here's exactly what to grab and how to run through the progression.

**What to Buy:**
* **Bench Grinder:** A silicon carbide grinding wheel (green wheel) for the initial rough shaping
* **Dremel Attachments:**
  * Silicon carbide sanding drums or a diamond burr assortment for shaping and contouring
  * A hook-and-loop backing pad mandrel, plus flexible sanding discs in these grits: 120, 220, 400, 600, 1200, and 3000
  * A felt polishing bob or wheel
* **Polishing Compound:** Cerium oxide powder, aluminum oxide polish, or diamond polishing paste (sub-micron, roughly 14,000–50,000 grit)

**The Progression:**

1. **Rough shaping (80–120 grit)** — Use the bench grinder's green wheel or coarse diamond burrs on the Dremel to block out your cabochon profile and establish the domed top.

2. **Medium shaping (220–400 grit)** — Switch to the 220-grit disc to knock out the deep gouges left by grinding, then move to 400 grit to refine the dome and smooth out scratches across that fibrous grain.

3. **Pre-polish (600–1200 grit)** — Run the 600-grit disc over the whole surface until it's smooth with a matte-to-satin look. Follow right away with 1200 grit to bring up a soft sheen.

4. **Fine pre-polish (3000 grit)** — Work this evenly across the stone to get it ready for the final optical polish.

5. **Final mirror polish** — Swap in the felt bob, load it with your aluminum oxide, cerium oxide, or diamond paste, and buff at medium speed with light-to-moderate pressure across the grain. Keep going until you've got that high-gloss, reflective shine.

Follow that sequence and you should have a beautiful, glassy cabochon ready well before Sunday. Your wife's going to love it.

This is such a sweet project—here's everything you need for the pattern and the machine setup to handle that thick double-layer fleece without a fight.

### 1. Pattern Outline & Measurements (0–3 / 3-Month Size)

These measurements already include a **1/2-inch seam allowance**, so you can cut straight from them:

* **Total Length:** 24 to 26 inches (shoulder to bottom hem).
* **Chest Width (underarm to underarm):** 11.5 to 12 inches across (about 23–24 inches total circumference).
* **Bottom Bag Width:** 16 to 18 inches across—this gives you that bell or pear shape that leaves room for kicking and hip movement.
* **Neck Opening:**
  * Width across the neck: 4.5 to 5 inches.
  * Front drop: 2 to 2.5 inches.
  * Back drop: 0.75 to 1 inch.
* **Armholes:**
  * Opening depth: 4 to 4.5 inches along the side curve (about 8.5–9 inches total circumference).
* **Shoulder Strap Width:** 2 to 2.5 inches wide.

**Drafting the shape:**
1. Start with a basic tank-top bodice using the chest, shoulder, and neck dimensions above.
2. From the base of the armhole, taper gradually outward into a wide, rounded bell shape toward the bottom.
3. Cut one back piece and either one front piece or two front halves if you want a center-front opening for the snaps.

### 2. Machine Settings for Thick, Stretchy Fleece

Pairing high-pile fleece with microfleece is going to want to slip and bunch, so here's how to keep it in line:

* **Needle:** A ballpoint or stretch needle, size 90/14 or 100/16. The rounded tip glides between the knit fibers instead of snagging, and the larger size punches cleanly through the pile.
* **Stitch type:** A narrow zigzag (0.5–1.0 mm width) or your machine's built-in stretch/lightning stitch—this lets the seam flex without popping.
* **Stitch length:** Lengthen it to 3.0–3.5 mm. Shorter stitches pack too much thread into thick fabric and cause wavy, bunched seams.
* **Tension:** Drop your upper thread tension a touch, from a standard 4 down to around 3 or 2.5, so the thread doesn't tunnel into the pile or pucker the fabric.

### 3. Tips for Feeding Double-Layer Fleece Smoothly

* **Use a walking foot (even feed foot).** It feeds the top and bottom layers at the same rate, so the top fleece won't creep ahead and bunch.
* **Loosen your presser foot pressure** if your machine allows it—this keeps the foot from dragging on the thick pile.
* **Pin generously.** Wonder Clips or long ball-head pins every 1–2 inches will keep both layers aligned as you sew.
* **Back your snap sites.** Fuse a small square of medium-weight woven interfacing or scrap cotton to the wrong side of the fleece under each snap location before you set it—this keeps the prongs from tearing through the stretchy knit.
* **Finish your edges cleanly.** Fleece won't fray, so you can simply fold the armhole and neckline edges under and stitch with a wide zigzag or twin needle, or bind them with lightweight knit bias tape to cut down on bulk.

Quick heads-up before the diagram: don't wire this between the amp head's speaker output and the cab. A standard Alpha pot is only rated for about 0.25–0.5W, while your Dual Rectifier's speaker output is pushing serious voltage and current into a 4–16Ω load. Put a 100k pot in that path and you'll fry the pot almost instantly, create an open-load condition, and risk taking out your amp's output transformer with it. Real speaker-level attenuation needs a high-wattage reactive or resistive load — think 50–100W wirewound resistors or a proper 8/16Ω power L-pad — not a guitar pot.

The good news: the pot box you've already built is perfect for a different job — an **effects loop master volume**. Wired between your preamp and power amp, it'll let you tame overall volume while still driving the poweramp the way you want. Here's how to hook it up.

### Wiring Diagram

Looking at the back of the 100k pot with the lugs pointing up (left to right: **1 – 2 – 3**):

```
       [ 100k Audio Pot ]
          (Rear View)
         [1]   [2]   [3]
          |     |     |
          |     |     +-----> Jack IN Tip (From Amp FX Send)
          |     +-----------> Jack OUT Tip (To Amp FX Return)
          +-----------------> Ground / Both Jack Sleeves & Enclosure
```

1. **Lug 3 (Input):** Wire to the **Tip** of the `IN` jack — this connects to the amp's **FX Send**.
2. **Lug 2 (Wiper/Output):** Wire to the **Tip** of the `OUT` jack — this connects to the amp's **FX Return**.
3. **Lug 1 (Ground):** Wire to the **Sleeve** of both jacks, and tie it to the metal enclosure for shielding.
4. **Jack Sleeves:** Connect together with a shared ground wire so both jacks share one ground reference.

### Putting It to Work

1. Run a cable from **Amp FX Send** into your **Box IN**.
2. Run another from your **Box OUT** into **Amp FX Return**.
3. Plug your speaker cab straight into the amp's speaker output, as usual.
4. Set your Dual Rectifier's Channel Master where you want that preamp saturation and tone, then use the box's pot to dial back the overall volume hitting the power amp — perfect for those quiet 2am sessions without losing the character of a cranked channel.

Hey, glad you're getting into this — but let's fix a couple things about the setup before you touch that grinder to your rough, because as planned it's going to cause you real problems.

First, dry grinding on a standard high-speed bench grinder (those run around 3450 RPM) is going to fight you the whole way. The heat from dry contact will thermal-shock the tiger's eye and can shatter it outright, and your vitrified grey wheel is going to glaze over almost immediately once you're loading it with stone dust instead of cutting cleanly.

Lapidary work really wants to be done wet and slower — somewhere in the 1725–1800 RPM range — with silicon carbide or diamond abrasives doing the cutting. If you want to adapt your current grinder rather than wait on the CabKing, here's what I'd do: pick up a router speed controller so you can dial the motor down to around 1750 RPM, and rig a simple drip system — a plastic bottle with an aquarium valve mounted above the wheel, dripping steadily onto the stone, with a catch basin below to deal with the runoff. That alone will change your results dramatically.

Here's the grit progression I'd follow once you've got water in the mix:

### Grit Progression & Technique

**1. Rough Shaping — 80–100 grit SiC**
Use your silicon carbide wheel with a continuous water drip. This is where you knock off the outer rind and rough in the dome or profile you're after. Work the stone in steady figure-eight motions across the face of the wheel — this keeps you from carving a groove into it. Expect to spend 5–15 minutes per piece here, depending on how hard the material is and how much you need to remove.

**2. Fine Shaping & Scratch Removal — 220 grit SiC**
Same wheel type, still wet. This step is about smoothing out the flat spots the 80 grit left behind. Dry the stone off completely and check it under a strong single light source — you want every trace of the 80-grit scratch pattern gone before you move forward. Usually 5–10 minutes does it.

**3. Pre-Polish / Smoothing — 400 to 600 grit**
Switch to flexible SiC sanding belts, discs, or expandable rubber drums, kept wet throughout. A hard vitrified wheel at this stage will leave you with stubborn flat spots, so avoid it here.
- *400 grit* clears out the 220 scratches and should leave a uniform matte surface — about 3–5 minutes.
- *600 grit* brings up a slight semi-gloss sheen. Double-check that no subsurface scratches remain before moving on — another 3–5 minutes.

**4. Pre-Polish — 1200 grit**
Leather, felt, or a 1200-grit wet belt will take you from that dull sheen to a smooth, low-luster surface that's ready for oxide polishing. This step is quick, usually just 2–3 minutes.

### Polishing & Compounds

For the final polish, run your hard felt buff damp — not soaking, not bone-dry — and keep the RPM on the lower side to avoid heat buildup. Tiger's eye will craze or crack if it gets too hot.

**For the tiger's eye:**
Cerium oxide or a high-purity aluminum oxide (Linde A) is what you want. Mix it with water to about the consistency of thin milk, brush it onto the felt buff, and apply moderate, even pressure. Keep the stone moving the whole time so you don't build up heat in one spot and burn the polish.

**For the chrysotile:**
Aluminum oxide works well here, and tin oxide is a good alternative. Use light pressure — this material is soft, and fibrous banding like yours can undercut easily if you press too hard or work it on a dry buff.

That should get you from rough chunks to polished pieces you'll be happy to display. Have fun with it.

Good news — you've got plenty of fruit to work with. Here's how the math shakes out:

### The Numbers & Yield
* **Fruit on hand:** 4 bushels of stone fruit works out to roughly **180–200 lbs**.
* **Natural sugar content:** Peaches and apricots typically ferment out to a wash around **5–6% ABV** on their own, no added sugar needed.
* **Fruit needed for 1 gallon of brandy:** To collect 1 gallon of finished 80–100 proof spirit (after you've made proper heads/tails cuts on your pot still), you generally need about **10–12 gallons of pure fruit wash**, which comes from roughly **80–100 lbs of crushed fruit**.

**Bottom line:** Your 180–200 lbs is more than enough — you're looking at about **1.5 to 2 gallons** of finished, proofed brandy from natural fruit sugars alone. You don't need to add table sugar unless you're trying to stretch your volume or push the wash up to 8–10% ABV (sometimes called a "sugar shine" or chaptalized fruit wash). Just keep in mind that leaning too hard on sugar will dilute the fruit character you're after.

---

### A Few Tips for Working with Stone Fruit

1. **Watch the pits.** Run your drill mixer in a way that mashes the flesh without cracking the stones open. Crushed pits release amygdalin, which can give your wash a harsh, bitter edge. Either pull the pits before mashing, or use a paddle at low speed that strips the flesh off without pulverizing them.

2. **Add pectic enzyme.** Stone fruit is loaded with pectin, and a dose of pectic enzyme before fermentation will break down the pulp, free up more juice, and boost your overall liquid yield.

3. **Plan for multiple runs.** With 10–20 gallons of fermented wash and a 3-gallon boiler, you'll need to do several stripping runs before combining the low wines into a final spirit run. Strain the liquid off the pulp as well as you can before distilling — it'll save you from scorching the bottom of the boiler.

You've got a solid setup here. With that much fruit, you're in good shape to end up with a nice batch of brandy.

You're really close to a solid setup — there's just one critical thing to verify before you mount anything: **you need to confirm the metal boxes themselves are actually tied back to ground.**

In houses from 1954, it's pretty common to find metal boxes fed by old two-wire cable with no bare ground wire, rather than grounded conduit or armored cable. If the box isn't actually connected back to the panel, screwing a pigtail into it won't give you a real equipment ground — it'll just be grounded to itself, which does nothing.

Here's how to check and finish the job right:

### 1. Test the Box for Ground (Takes About 30 Seconds)

Grab a digital multimeter (or a basic two-lead voltage tester):

1. Restore power to the circuit.
2. Put one test lead on the **hot wire** (usually black) and the other on **bare metal of the box** (scratch a small clean spot if it's painted or dusty).
3. **Read the result:**
   - **~120V:** Great news — your metal box is grounded, likely through metallic conduit or armored cable. Your plan to use the green grounding pigtails in the threaded hole on the back of the box is exactly right, and you're good to go on all six outlets.
   - **0V:** The box isn't grounded. Just attaching a pigtail here will create a "floating ground" that looks right but won't actually protect your gear.

### 2. If the Box Isn't Grounded: Your Best Options

**Option A: Install a GFCI Receptacle (fastest, code-compliant)**
Under the National Electrical Code, you're allowed to replace two-prong outlets on an ungrounded circuit with three-prong ones as long as you protect them with a GFCI receptacle at the first outlet in the run (or a GFCI breaker at the panel).
- Wire the GFCI using just hot and neutral.
- Use the little blue "No Equipment Ground" stickers that come in the GFCI box, and put one on each faceplate downstream.
- One thing worth knowing for your setup: a GFCI protects you from shock beautifully, but surge protectors need a true equipment ground to actually shunt voltage spikes away from your gear. So this option keeps you safe, but it doesn't give your OLED and receiver the full protection a real ground would.

**Option B: Run New Cable (best option for high-end AV gear)**
Since your walls are already open, this is genuinely the best time to run new NM-B cable (14/2 or 12/2 with ground) straight from the panel to these living room outlets. It gives you a true, dedicated equipment ground — which is what you want behind a setup like this, both for surge protection and for keeping noise out of your audio gear.

Do that quick meter check on the first box and you'll know exactly which path you're on — then you can move through the rest of the outlets with confidence.
